draft.title: Derivatives of exponentials and logarithms
card: The derivative of eˣ is eˣ. For a general power, use the chain rule: the derivative of e^f(x) is f'(x) × e^f(x).
The derivative of ln x is 1/x. In general, the derivative of ln f(x) is f'(x)/f(x), which is the derivative of the inside divided by the inside.
Example: for y = e^(3x²), the inside is 3x², with derivative 6x. So dy/dx = 6x × e^(3x²).
Example: for y = ln(x² + 1), the inside is x² + 1, with derivative 2x. So dy/dx = 2x/(x² + 1).
draft.remember: Find the derivative of the inside. Multiply it by e^f(x), or put it over f(x) for ln.

a.q: What is the derivative of e^(5x)?
a.why: The inside is 5x, with derivative 5. So the derivative is 5 × e^(5x). Leaving out the 5 is tempting because eˣ is its own derivative, but the chain rule needs the derivative of the inside.
a.clue: Multiply by the derivative of the power.

b.q: Mia is given y = ln(x³ + 4x). What is dy/dx?
b.why: The inside is x³ + 4x, with derivative 3x² + 4. The derivative of ln f(x) is f'(x)/f(x), so the answer is (3x² + 4)/(x³ + 4x). Writing only 1/(x³ + 4x) skips the derivative of the inside.
b.clue: Put the derivative of the inside on top.

final.title: Derivatives of exponentials and logarithms
card: The derivative of \(e^{x}\) is \(e^{x}\). For a general power, use the chain rule: the derivative of \(e^{f(x)}\) is \(f'(x) \times e^{f(x)}\).
The derivative of \(\ln x\) is \(\frac{1}{x}\). In general, the derivative of \(\ln f(x)\) is \(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\), which is the derivative of the inside divided by the inside.
Example: for \(y = e^{3x^{2}}\), the inside is \(3x^{2}\), with derivative \(6x\). So \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 6x \times e^{3x^{2}}\).
Example: for \(y = \ln(x^{2} + 1)\), the inside is \(x^{2} + 1\), with derivative \(2x\). So \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2x}{x^{2} + 1}\).
final.remember: Find the derivative of the inside. Multiply it by \(e^{f(x)}\), or put it over \(f(x)\) for \(\ln f(x)\).

a.why: The inside is \(5x\), with derivative 5. So the derivative is \(5 \times e^{5x}\). Leaving out the 5 is tempting because \(e^{x}\) is its own derivative, but the chain rule needs the derivative of the inside.
a.clue: Multiply by the derivative of the power.

b.why: The inside is \(x^{3} + 4x\), with derivative \(3x^{2} + 4\). The derivative of \(\ln f(x)\) is \(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\), so the answer is \(\frac{3x^{2} + 4}{x^{3} + 4x}\). Writing only \(\frac{1}{x^{3} + 4x}\) skips the derivative of the inside.
b.clue: Put the derivative of the inside on top.
